theory.intro: A **fractional index** is another way of writing a root. The denominator says which root to take and the numerator says which power to raise to, so $27^{\frac{2}{3}}$ means the cube root of $27$, then squared. Every index law still applies when the bases are positive. Symbolic bases in the exercises are assumed positive unless otherwise specified. A base must be nonzero when its index is negative.
facts: $a^{\frac{1}{n}}=\sqrt[n]{a}$ — root indices $n$ are positive integers. For even $n$, require $a\geq0$; for odd $n$, any real $a$ is allowed. The denominator of the index is the index of the root, so $64^{\frac{1}{3}}=\sqrt[3]{64}$.

$a^{\frac{1}{n}}=\sqrt[n]{a}$ — root indices $n$ are positive integers. For even $n$, require $a\geq0$; for odd $n$, any real $a$ is allowed. The denominator of the index is the index of the root, so $64^{\frac{1}{3}}=\sqrt[3]{64}=4$.

For a positive base $a$, an integer numerator $m$ and a positive integer denominator $n$, $a^{\frac{m}{n}}=\sqrt[n]{a^{m}}=\left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^{m}$ — take the root named by the denominator, then raise to the numerator. For example $27^{\frac{2}{3}}=\left(\sqrt[3]{27}\right)^2=9$.

For positive bases, the index laws hold for fractional indices — add when multiplying, subtract when dividing, multiply when raising a power to a power: $x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times x^{\frac{1}{3}}=x^{\frac{5}{6}}$ for $x>0$.
For a negative numerical base, an odd root gives a real value, for example $(-8)^{\frac{1}{3}}=-2$. An even root of a negative number has no real value.
steps: Deal with a negative index first by writing the reciprocal.
Take the root named by the denominator of the index.
Raise that result to the power named by the numerator.

workedExamples.question_text: Evaluate $49^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, giving your answer as a fraction.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Deal with the negative index first.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}49^{-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\frac{1}{49^{\frac{1}{2}}}\\&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{49}}\\&=\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}$

Take the fourth root, then cube the result.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}625^{\frac{3}{4}}\\&=\left(\sqrt[4]{625}\right)^3\\&=5^3\\&=125\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Evaluate $64^{-\frac{5}{6}}$, giving your answer as a fraction.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Take the cube root of the numerator and denominator, then square.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\left(\frac{125}{216}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\\&=\left(\frac{\sqrt[3]{125}}{\sqrt[3]{216}}\right)^2\\&=\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2\\&=\frac{25}{36}\end{aligned}$

Invert the fraction first, then take the fourth root and cube.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\left(\frac{16}{625}\right)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\\&=\left(\frac{625}{16}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}\\&=\left(\frac{\sqrt[4]{625}}{\sqrt[4]{16}}\right)^3\\&=\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^3\\&=\frac{125}{8}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Simplify $r^{\frac{2}{5}}\times r^{\frac{1}{3}}$, leaving your answer in index form. Assume $r>0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Add the indices when multiplying powers with the same base.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}r^{\frac{2}{5}}\times r^{\frac{1}{3}}\\&=r^{\frac{2}{5}+\frac{1}{3}}\\&=r^{\frac{6}{15}+\frac{5}{15}}\\&=r^{\frac{11}{15}}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Simplify $s^{\frac{7}{8}}\div s^{\frac{1}{4}}$, leaving your answer in index form. Assume $s>0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Subtract the indices when dividing powers with the same base.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}s^{\frac{7}{8}}\div s^{\frac{1}{4}}\\&=s^{\frac{7}{8}-\frac{1}{4}}\\&=s^{\frac{7}{8}-\frac{2}{8}}\\&=s^{\frac{5}{8}}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Simplify $\left(u^{\frac{5}{6}}\right)^3$, leaving your answer in index form. Assume $u>0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Multiply the indices when raising a power to a power.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\left(u^{\frac{5}{6}}\right)^3\\&=u^{\frac{5}{6}\times3}\\&=u^{\frac{15}{6}}\\&=u^{\frac{5}{2}}\end{aligned}$

Apply the outside index to each factor.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\left(243v^{10}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}\\&=243^{\frac{1}{5}}v^{10\times\frac{1}{5}}\\&=3v^2\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Simplify $\left(z^{\frac{3}{5}}\right)^2\times z^{\frac{1}{3}}\div z^{\frac{1}{2}}$, leaving your answer in index form. Assume $z>0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Multiply the indices in the bracket first, then add and subtract the remaining indices.

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\left(z^{\frac{3}{5}}\right)^2\times z^{\frac{1}{3}}\div z^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=z^{\frac{6}{5}}\times z^{\frac{1}{3}}\div z^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=z^{\frac{6}{5}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=z^{\frac{36}{30}+\frac{10}{30}-\frac{15}{30}}\\&=z^{\frac{31}{30}}\end{aligned}$

Adding the indices gives the resulting power. Since $a>0$ and $a\ne1$, equal powers of $a$ have equal indices.

$\begin{aligned}n&=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{2}{5}\\n&=\frac{15}{20}+\frac{8}{20}\\n&=\frac{23}{20}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Explain why $(-81)^{\frac{1}{4}}$ has no real value.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}(-81)^{\frac{1}{4}}\\&=\sqrt[4]{-81}\end{aligned}$

Every real number has a non-negative fourth power. No real number has fourth power $-81$, so the expression has no real value.

Explain why $(-16)^{\frac{1}{4}}$ has no real value.
foundation.solution_text:
$(-16)^{\frac{1}{4}}$
$=\sqrt[4]{-16}$
Raising any real number to the power $4$ gives a non-negative result, so no real number has a fourth power of $-16$ and the expression has no real value.
